II · ECDLP

III. From an elliptic-curve key to a Fourier sample

Equal point outputs connect scalar inputs along a hidden direction. Fourier sampling reveals that direction; window tables supply the point arithmetic that makes the oracle practical.

8 min core readingp. 7 · p. 8Coverage & audit

Two moduli, one hidden relation

We know two curve points, PPP and Q=[d]PQ=[d]PQ=[d]P, and want the hidden scalar ddd. Point multiples repeat modulo the order rrr of PPP, while their coordinates use a different prime ppp. The curve equation below defines those coordinates; the quantum algorithm extracts a relation between scalar labels.

E: y2=x3+7(modp),p=2256−(232+977). E:\ y^2=x^3+7\pmod p,\qquad p=2^{256}-(2^{32}+977). E: y2=x3+7(modp),p=2256−(232+977).

Evaluate f(k,l)=[k]P+[l]Q=[k+dl]Pf(k,l)=[k]P+[l]Q=[k+dl]Pf(k,l)=[k]P+[l]Q=[k+dl]P. Different pairs (k,l)(k,l)(k,l) can produce the same point whenever k+dlk+dlk+dl agrees modulo rrr. That is the useful structure: equality of outputs groups the input labels along a direction determined by the secret.

What the three register labels mean

We use two input registers for k,lk,lk,l and an accumulator AAA for the point. To see the Fourier relation cleanly, first imagine labels in Zr\mathbb Z_rZr​. The physical qubit registers instead have mmm bits and contain labels from 0 to 2m−12^m-12m−1, with mmm chosen relative to n=⌈log⁡2r⌉n=\lceil\log_2r\rceiln=⌈log2​r⌉.

LabelMathematical valueStorage in the logical arithmetic circuit
k,lk,lk,lBinary integers whose point multiples depend only on their residue modulo rrrTwo mmm-qubit scalar registers in the clean theoretical circuit. The implementation later measures and reuses small window registers.
AAAOne curve pointTwo field-element registers, A=(xA,yA)A=(x_A,y_A)A=(xA​,yA​), each containing 256 logical qubits. Fault-tolerant encoding stores the logical qubits collectively in larger physical code blocks. “One point register” therefore bundles two coordinate registers. This is the chosen affine representation, not an information-theoretic lower bound on storing a point.

The ideal accumulator begins at the identity O\mathcal OO. The implementation starts at a known random nonzero point and shifts the lookup tables. This avoids identity entries and distributes the remaining exceptional additions. The final constant translation affects only the point register, leaving the input Fourier statistics unchanged.

A line becomes a Fourier constraint

Suppose the point register has value [c]P[c]P[c]P. The compatible inputs satisfy k=c−dlk=c-dlk=c−dl, so they form a uniform line of labels. Apply the inverse Fourier transform to both inputs, using Fr∣a⟩=r−1/2∑ue2πiau/r∣u⟩F_r|a\rangle=r^{-1/2}\sum_u e^{2\pi iau/r}|u\rangleFr​∣a⟩=r−1/2∑u​e2πiau/r∣u⟩. The transform turns that line into a constraint on measured frequencies.

Move the coset; the Fourier line stays put

Choose a secret and move the output-point slider. The input pairs move to a different parallel line. After the Fourier transform, the same frequencies survive: their line reveals the secret.

To see this exactly, use r=7r=7r=7, with seven states per register. Solid circles mark outcomes of probability 1/71/71/7; small dots have probability zero. Seven-state registers give the ideal group transform; the binary registers in the full algorithm broaden these peaks.

Suppose the target contains the point [c]P[c]P[c]P: its compatible inputs obey k+dl=c(mod7)k+dl=c\pmod7k+dl=c(mod7). Here c labels that point; the target register holds its coordinates. Every possible target outcome gives a line of this form. We can therefore analyze one line at a time, whether or not we actually measure the target.

v=du(mod7)v=du\pmod7v=du(mod7)

For d = 3, changing c moves the input coset but leaves the Fourier probabilities unchanged.

The point label appears only in phase. The secret determines the surviving line: any measured u≠0u\ne0u=0 gives d=vu−1(mod7)d=vu^{-1}\pmod7d=vu−1(mod7).

For general order rrr: why only one frequency line survives

The state below shows this conversion explicitly. Conditioning on the point makes the line visible in the derivation; measuring the point is optional because tracing it out gives the same input statistics.

∣ψc⟩=1r∑l∣c−dl,l⟩→Fr†⊗Fr†1r∑ue−2πicu/r∣u,du⟩. |\psi_c\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_l|c-dl,l\rangle \xrightarrow{F_r^\dagger\otimes F_r^\dagger} \frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_u e^{-2\pi icu/r}|u,du\rangle. ∣ψc​⟩=r​1​l∑​∣c−dl,l⟩Fr†​⊗Fr†​​r​1​u∑​e−2πicu/r∣u,du⟩.

At frequency pair (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), the terms along the line contribute ∑le2πil(du−v)/r\sum_l e^{2\pi il(du-v)/r}∑l​e2πil(du−v)/r. They add when v=duv=duv=du and cancel otherwise. The offset ccc contributes only a phase. Thus a nonzero uuu lets us recover d=vu−1(modr)d=vu^{-1}\pmod rd=vu−1(modr).

Qubits broaden the peaks

A qubit register has size M=2mM=2^mM=2m, so its finite lines do not fit the group period exactly. Their Fourier peaks broaden. Another way to describe the same process is two phase estimates of commuting translations by PPP and QQQ. They share a uniformly sampled eigenlabel sss, with phases

θ1=s/r,θ2=(ds mod r)/r. \theta_1=s/r,\qquad \theta_2=(ds\bmod r)/r. θ1​=s/r,θ2​=(dsmodr)/r.

With enough precision, rounding the two estimates recovers their integer numerators and hence the secret. Mosca's bound quantifies this event. Ekerå's search uses nearby candidates to recover additional samples and accommodate shorter controls.

First do the computation classically

We next need a circuit for the point-valued function. Begin classically: divide each scalar into windows of www bits,

k=∑iki2iw,l=∑ili2iw,0≤ki,li<2w.k=\sum_i k_i2^{iw},\qquad l=\sum_i l_i2^{iw},\qquad 0\le k_i,l_i<2^w.k=i∑​ki​2iw,l=i∑​li​2iw,0≤ki​,li​<2w.
Each digit chooses one precomputed multiple of PPP or QQQ. The position of the window determines the table, and its digit determines the row.

For each position iii, compute the tables

Ti(P)[j]=[j2iw]P,Ti(Q)[j]=[j2iw]Q.T_i^{(P)}[j]=[j2^{iw}]P,\qquad T_i^{(Q)}[j]=[j2^{iw}]Q.Ti(P)​[j]=[j2iw]P,Ti(Q)​[j]=[j2iw]Q.
before the quantum run. The schedule knows iii; only the row address is quantum. This replaces many bit-controlled point additions by one table selection and one addition per window.

Every entry is a known coordinate pair. Computing multiples of the public point QQQ does not require knowing ddd. The two-bit example below shows the first few tables explicitly, so we can follow how their place values combine.

Address jWindow 0: T₀[j]Window 1: T₁[j]

For k=11=3+4⋅2k=11=3+4\cdot2k=11=3+4⋅2, use row 3 of the first table and row 2 of the second. The accumulator goes from O\mathcal OO to [3]P[3]P[3]P, then to [11]P[11]P[11]P. Applying the same procedure to lll and the Q tables produces [k]P+[l]Q[k]P+[l]Q[k]P+[l]Q. The actual 16-bit tables each have 65,536 rows.

The example uses unshifted tables for clarity. In the implementation, each table receives a known offset RiR_iRi​ chosen to exclude O\mathcal OO, and the accumulator starts at A0≠OA_0\ne\mathcal OA0​=O. All outputs acquire the same translation A0+∑iRiA_0+\sum_iR_iA0​+∑i​Ri​. This preserves the Fourier relation while the failure analysis accounts for the remaining exceptional additions.

What one accumulator update computes

One update adds two points, (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​) and (x2,y2)(x_2,y_2)(x2​,y2​). On the nonexceptional branch, compute their slope and then the new coordinates:

λ=(y1−y2)(x1−x2)−1,x3=λ2−x1−x2,y3=λ(x2−x3)−y2.\lambda=(y_1-y_2)(x_1-x_2)^{-1},\qquad x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2,\qquad y_3=\lambda(x_2-x_3)-y_2.λ=(y1​−y2​)(x1​−x2​)−1,x3​=λ2−x1​−x2​,y3​=λ(x2​−x3​)−y2​.
These formulas identify the required arithmetic: field division, square subtraction, and multiplication.

Field division is where gcd enters. Euclid gives aΔx+bp=1a\Delta x+bp=1aΔx+bp=1, making aaa the inverse of the nonzero coordinate difference. The paper applies that inverse through recorded reductions. The point-addition lesson then arranges the formulas so temporary values can be cleared without revealing the selected address.

Now make the lookup coherent

Now promote the row address to a www-qubit register. The table remains classical data compiled into gates. If Fi(j)F_i(j)Fi​(j) is the coordinate bit string for row jjj, load it by XOR into a target register:

Li:∣j⟩∣z⟩⟼∣j⟩∣z⊕Fi(j)⟩.L_i:|j\rangle|z\rangle\longmapsto |j\rangle|z\oplus F_i(j)\rangle.Li​:∣j⟩∣z⟩⟼∣j⟩∣z⊕Fi​(j)⟩.
This operation preserves the address and is reversible for every initial target value.

Starting the target at zero loads the selected word. Applying the same XOR lookup again clears it. On a superposition of addresses, linearity gives

∑jαj∣j⟩∣0⟩⟼∑jαj∣j⟩∣Fi(j)⟩.\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|0\rangle\longmapsto\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|F_i(j)\rangle.j∑​αj​∣j⟩∣0⟩⟼j∑​αj​∣j⟩∣Fi​(j)⟩.
This is a coherent lookup, not the point addition itself: the latter acts on the loaded coordinates afterward.

The lookup never asks a classical processor to read the address. Each basis branch follows its corresponding table row, so the address and output can become entangled while preserving the interference needed by the algorithm.

Inside the lookup: a complete two-bit example

The next diagram exposes every gate for a two-bit address and a two-bit output word f1f0f_1f_0f1​f0​. It is a small data table chosen to illustrate lookup mechanics; the full coordinate word has 512 bits.

Address j₁j₀Stored word f₁f₀Output bits to flip
0001z₀
0110z₁
1011z₁ and z₀
1100None

For address 10, only the final two gates fire and write 11. In a superposition, the same gate sequence applies the appropriate row to every branch. Starting from an arbitrary output zzz produces z⊕f(j)z\oplus f(j)z⊕f(j), which also shows why the circuit is reversible.

How this scales to a long coordinate word

For a long output word, repeatedly testing the full address for each output bit wastes work. Compute the row selector a=[j=t]a=[j=t]a=[j=t] once, use it to flip every 1 in the constant row, then clear it. The selector's cost is shared across the entire word.

Unary lookup also shares partial address tests between neighboring rows. The compiler overlaps two such traversals in its zipper schedule. Both changes preserve the XOR contract. The diagram shows compute–copy–uncompute; measurement with phase repair can replace part of the cleanup.

The shared-test circuit behind unary lookup

At one node of the traversal, let ccc enable the subtree and xxx choose its branch. Compute a=cxa=cxa=cx and use it to load word D1D_1D1​. A CNOT changes it to c(1−x)c(1-x)c(1−x), enabling D0D_0D0​. Restore the AND value, then erase it by X measurement and conditional CZ. One AND has served both branches and every output bit.

The full lookup sequence expands this node into an eight-entry table, then into the two controlled 15-bit traversals used by the paper. It also shows the block relays and phase repair needed when coordinate outputs are cleared.

Use the loaded point, then clear it

With lookup available, the following circuit loads a point, adds it to the accumulator, and clears the loaded word. Each point wire contains two coordinate registers. This gives the logical construction before optimizing when its workspace is released.

The optimized addition loads coordinates three times because their workspace is needed between uses. The first lookup forms coordinate differences; the second supplies 3x23x_23x2​ for square subtraction; the third removes the final offsets. X measurements free each output early and a later phase lookup repairs their signs. The cleanup circuit follows this reuse explicitly.

ChangeWhat it savesWhat it costs
16-bit windowsOne addition per window2162^{16}216-entry lookups
Direct first lookupThe first additionA separately charged initialization
Omit three windowsThree more additions; 28 remainClassical recovery of 48 missing bits
Measure and reuse controlsTwo persistent scalar registersAdaptive Fourier rotations and feedforward

The conservative Fourier branch adds one control bit per scalar, making the initial direct lookup contain 2182^{18}218 entries. Later windows remain 16 bits. Once a window has been used and Fourier-measured, its controls can be reset while the point accumulator stays coherent.

Notation and physical meaning

Definitions are also given where they are used. Open the full notation page.

ppp — field prime
Coordinates lie in the finite field Fp\mathbb F_pFp​, the integers modulo ppp. For secp256k1, p=2256−232−977p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977p=2256−232−977. This modulus controls coordinate arithmetic. Use in the construction
ppp — local error probability
On architecture and state-preparation pages, ppp is the error probability specified beside the formula: for example, a physical two-qubit Pauli error rate or an injected-state fault rate. Each model defines the event and operation counted. Arithmetic pages instead use ppp for the field prime. Use in the construction
rrr — subgroup order
The number of distinct multiples of the generator point PPP; [r]P=O[r]P=\mathcal O[r]P=O. Scalar recovery is modulo rrr, not the field prime ppp. Use in the construction
ddd — secret scalar
The unknown element of Zr\mathbb Z_rZr​ satisfying Q=[d]PQ=[d]PQ=[d]P. Recovering it is the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem. Use in the construction
P,Q,OP,Q,\mathcal OP,Q,O — curve points
PPP is the chosen generator, QQQ is the public input point, and O\mathcal OO is the identity element of the curve group. [a]P[a]P[a]P denotes repeated point addition. Use in the construction
ccc — small prime offset
p=2n−cp=2^n-cp=2n−c, so 2n≡c(modp)2^n\equiv c\pmod p2n≡c(modp). For secp256k1, n=256n=256n=256 and c=232+977c=2^{32}+977c=232+977. This relation makes reduction of high bits cheap. Use in the construction
www — scalar-window width
The number of scalar bits handled by one coherent point lookup. The main loop uses w=16w=16w=16, giving tables indexed by 16-bit addresses. Use in the construction
λ\lambdaλ — point-addition slope
For distinct affine points with different x coordinates, λ=(y2−y1)/(x2−x1)\lambda=(y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1)λ=(y2​−y1​)/(x2​−x1​) in Fp\mathbb F_pFp​. The division means multiplication by a modular inverse. Elsewhere the same Greek letter may denote a Poisson mean; each lesson specifies its domain. Use in the construction
pfp_fpf​ — approximate-oracle failure bound
For each fixed input pair, an upper bound over fresh random masks on producing either wrong coordinates or a wrong relative phase. Appendix B obtains pf≤0.03346p_f\le0.03346pf​≤0.03346. Use in the construction
P0P_0P0​ — ideal algorithm success
Success probability assigned to exact arithmetic with the selected quantum Fourier measurement and classical recovery procedure. The rigorous and heuristic starting estimates must be kept separate. Use in the construction
QFT / iQFT — quantum Fourier transform
A unitary change of basis between a modular coordinate and its phase frequency. iQFT denotes its inverse. Measuring the result exposes the periodic relation used to recover the secret scalar. Use in the construction
CCX — Toffoli gate
The three-bit reversible map (a,b,t)↦(a,b,t⊕ab)(a,b,t)\mapsto(a,b,t\oplus ab)(a,b,t)↦(a,b,t⊕ab). It is a controlled-controlled-X gate and the main non-Clifford logical resource of the arithmetic. Use in the construction
CCZ — controlled-controlled-Z
The three-qubit unitary ∣a,b,c⟩↦(−1)abc∣a,b,c⟩|a,b,c\rangle\mapsto(-1)^{abc}|a,b,c\rangle∣a,b,c⟩↦(−1)abc∣a,b,c⟩. Conjugating its third qubit by Hadamards gives a Toffoli. A CCZ resource state is CCZ∣+⟩⊗3\mathrm{CCZ}|+\rangle^{\otimes3}CCZ∣+⟩⊗3. Use in the construction
TTT — pi-over-four phase gate
T=diag⁡(1,eiπ/4)T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})T=diag(1,eiπ/4). A T state, up to the convention specified in a lesson, supplies this non-Clifford phase through state injection. The symbol TTT also denotes time in resource equations, where units are explicit. Use in the construction
Clifford frame — tracked logical transformation
A Clifford unitary maps Pauli operators to Pauli operators by conjugation. Instead of applying every such gate physically, the controller can track the accumulated map and reinterpret later measurements. Use in the construction
CliNR — Clifford noise-reduction protocol
Logical CliNR uses a prepared, checked Clifford resource and teleportation. Here it is used to clear a complicated tracked Clifford frame and restore simple logical-measurement representatives. Use in the construction
Q102 — main memory code
The quantum code [[102,22,9]][[102,22,9]][[102,22,9]]: 102 data qubits encode 22 logical qubits with distance 9. Device counts additionally include syndrome ancillas and replacement ions. Use in the construction
Q66 — factory code
The quantum code [[66,4,10]][[66,4,10]][[66,4,10]]: 66 data qubits encode four logical qubits with distance 10. It protects the CCZ-factory state and supports the specific representatives tabulated in Appendix G. Use in the construction
C6 — six-qubit detection code
The [[6,2,2]][[6,2,2]][[6,2,2]] code encodes two logical qubits. In the factory it prepares a pair of low-error logical H states using error detection and postselection. Use in the construction
Cat state — shared parity-measurement resource
A length-m cat is (∣0⟩⊗m+∣1⟩⊗m)/2(|0\rangle^{\otimes m}+|1\rangle^{\otimes m})/\sqrt2(∣0⟩⊗m+∣1⟩⊗m)/2​. Each cat qubit touches at most one target qubit when measuring a product Pauli operator, limiting fault spread. Use in the construction
POC — physical operation cycle
The basic physical timing unit used in the architecture, 0.2 ms0.2\,\mathrm{ms}0.2ms. Gate, transport, and syndrome schedules are expressed in these units. Use in the construction
SEC — syndrome-extraction cycle
One repeated measurement of the code's error checks with its physical schedule. Q102 takes 27 POCs per SEC; Q66 takes 17 POCs per SEC under the stated architecture. Use in the construction
LM / LM2 — logical measurement
LM denotes a measurement of a logical Pauli operator. LM2 spans two code blocks and requires resources that join their local cat states. A logical operation can take several SECs to achieve enough readout confidence. Use in the construction
supp⁡(P)\operatorname{supp}(P)supp(P) — Pauli support
The physical qubits on which a Pauli string PPP acts as X, Y, or Z rather than I. Its cardinality is the operator weight. Commuting operators need not have disjoint supports. Use in the construction
Logical representative — physical realization of an encoded Pauli
Different physical Pauli strings can implement the same logical operation because multiplying by a stabilizer leaves the encoded action unchanged. Choosing representatives controls weight and parallel compatibility. Use in the construction
gcd — greatest common divisor
The largest integer dividing two inputs. Binary-gcd updates use parity tests, subtraction, and division by two. Recording and replaying these updates implements modular multiplication or division reversibly. Use in the construction
κ\kappaκ — truncated carry width
The number of low bits through which a small modular correction is allowed to propagate. A carry beyond that range is one of the approximate arithmetic failure events. Use in the construction
DmeasD_{\rm meas}Dmeas​ — charged measurement depth
The sum of scheduled logical-measurement layers, including the expected penalties used in the resource accounting: 75,251,329 for the reported computation. Use in the construction
τ\tauτ — seconds per charged layer
Appendix E23 uses the unrounded value 0.0294958 s0.0294958\,\mathrm{s}0.0294958s. Table I displays it as 29.50 ms. Runtime is DmeasτD_{\rm meas}\tauDmeas​τ. Use in the construction
Postselection — accept only verified preparations
A preparation attempt is retained only if specified measurement checks pass; otherwise it restarts. Output error is conditioned on acceptance, and retries affect throughput. Use in the construction
pswapp_{\rm swap}pswap​ — survivor-displacement probability
Conditional on a two-qubit interaction involving a loss, the probability that the surviving ion is displaced to the other position. It is not the ordinary two-qubit Pauli error probability. Use in the construction
